find: Open the deck by naming the elephant. AI coding tools (Claude, Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, every frontier model) are now in production engineering workflows. They produce code fluently. From a one-sentence prompt they will produce a microservices decomposition, a saga, a cache layer, a strangler fig wrapper, a CQRS write side: plausible enough to compile, deploy and run. The risk is also new: a developer who doesn't have the vocabulary to evaluate what comes back is rolling dice in production. The patterns in this deck are not nostalgic computer-science trivia; they are the literacy that lets you direct AI tooling instead of being directed by it. Walk the three layers of patterns briefly: design patterns are code-level vocabulary (Gang of Four); architecture patterns describe how applications fit together (hexagonal, microservices, BFF, event-driven); system design patterns, the focus of this deck, span services, data and runtime (sagas, caching, the strangler fig, outbox, decomposition, L7 routing). The four maxims are the philosophical spine. ‘Least-worst decision’: every architecture choice is a set of trades (latency for throughput, consistency for availability, simplicity for flexibility), and the job is not to find the optionless option but to make the trades visible and explicit. ‘Risk management’: you manage the distribution of failures, not their existence. ‘No free lunch’: every pattern (cache, saga, eventing, decomposition) has a cost — a stale read window, a compensation path, a coordination tax, an operational complexity. The question is whether you are buying the right thing for what you are paying. ‘No problem cannot be made worse’ is the warning corollary: a confidently-wrong intervention amplifies the original pain, and AI tooling makes confident interventions fast and cheap. The closing line is the audience take-home: AI is the amplifier; the patterns are the literacy that decides which direction it amplifies.

find: Each of the four tools does a different job. Kafka is the substrate: a partitioned, ordered, durable log. Consumers track their own offsets and can replay. It's the de facto event spine for cloud-native architectures; Strimzi runs it natively on Kubernetes. Pulsar is also substrate, in the same broad category as Kafka but with native pub/sub plus queue semantics in the same product, tiered storage that pushes cold data to cheap object stores automatically, and multi-tenancy built into the broker. Pulsar has a Kafka-protocol shim so consumers can speak Kafka while writing to Pulsar. Flink is compute: not a transport layer, but a stateful stream-processing engine. Flink sits on top of Kafka or Pulsar, consumes streams, applies operators (windowed aggregations, joins, filters, stateful transformations) with exactly-once semantics via checkpointing, and produces new streams. Alternatives: Kafka Streams (lighter, JVM-only, embedded library), Spark Structured Streaming (heavier, batch-mindset). NiFi is movement: a visual dataflow / ETL tool with 200+ source-and-sink connectors and back-pressure built in. Think of it as the answer to 'I need to get data from SFTP to Kafka to an object store with these transforms in the middle' — you draw the flow in the UI rather than writing a pipeline. Debezium (covered in the Data section) is the CDC variant of movement. Together they compose: typical pipeline is source DB → Debezium or NiFi → Kafka or Pulsar → Flink for windowed aggregations → sink. The mistake is treating these as competitors. They complement each other; pick by the question your team is asking: durably hold events (substrate), compute over them (Flink), move them around (NiFi/Debezium).

find: The cost-control reality: at scale you cannot store every trace, so you sample. The key question is when the keep/drop decision is made. Head sampling decides at the start, in the SDK, before the trace even completes — typically 'keep 1 in N' (probabilistic) or 'keep N per second' (rate-limiting). It's cheap and low-overhead, but it is blind at decision time: it can't keep a trace because it errored or was slow, because it decides before knowing. Tail sampling decides at the end, in the Collector, after the whole trace has been seen — the Collector buffers spans, waits for the trace to complete, then applies rules: keep all errors, keep all traces over 500ms, keep rare routes, sample the boring successful ones at 1%. Tail is smart but costs memory (buffering in-flight traces) and CPU (the Collector does real work). The strategies, named: probabilistic (keep X%), rate-limiting (cap per second), parent-based (follow the upstream's decision so a trace isn't half-sampled), and tail rules (error / latency / attribute based). The common production setup is both: a parent-based head sample for a representative baseline, plus tail sampling at the Collector to guarantee every error and every slow trace is captured regardless of the baseline rate. Two rules to drill home: always sample by trace, not by span (a half-sampled trace is worse than no trace), and propagate the sampling flag (the 01 in traceparent) so every service agrees. Metrics and logs are usually not sampled the same way: metrics aggregate everything (you don't sample a counter), and logs are typically kept in full with retention limits or sampled on their own policy.

find: The vocabulary clarification most teams need before they go further with events. Event sourcing means events are the database — there is no 'current state' row anywhere; current state is computed by folding the entire event history. Adding a credit to an account isn't UPDATE balance SET balance = balance + 100; it's INSERT INTO events VALUES ('credit', 100), and reading the balance means summing every event for that account (with snapshots for performance). Strong fit for audit-heavy systems (banking, healthcare records, regulatory), temporal queries ("what was the balance on March 3rd?"), and any domain where the history is itself a primary asset. Tools: Marten (Postgres-backed, .NET), EventStoreDB, Axon (JVM). Event streaming means events are how facts move between services — each service still keeps its current state in a normal database, but emits events ("order.placed", "payment.processed") that other services subscribe to. The event is a transport mechanism, not a storage mechanism. Strong fit for integration, fan-out, decoupling. Tools: Kafka, Pulsar, NATS JetStream. These are not mutually exclusive. A common combination is full CQRS: the write side is event-sourced (so you have an audit trail of state changes), and the read-side projections are fed by streaming those events to consumers that build denormalised views. The acid test: is the event itself the source of truth (sourcing), or is it a propagated fact about a change that happened in a store (streaming)? In most enterprise architectures, streaming is far more common than sourcing; sourcing fits domains where audit and replay are core.

find: The mechanism that makes CQRS projections and the outbox pattern work: Change Data Capture, or CDC. The application writes ordinary SQL. The database commits and the change lands in the write-ahead log (WAL on Postgres, redo log on Oracle, binlog on MySQL, transaction log on SQL Server). Debezium, an Apache 2.0 open-source project running as a set of Kafka Connect connectors, tails that log via the database's native replication protocol (logical replication slots on Postgres, etc.), translates row-level deltas into Kafka events, and publishes them with commit ordering preserved. The application doesn't know Debezium exists. There is no dual-write — the commit is the single source of truth, and the event is a strictly downstream consequence. This is why log tailing matters before the outbox: the outbox is a targeted use of CDC for a specific case (publishing events that aren't naturally row-level), and CQRS projections are the other big use. Debezium supports Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle, MongoDB, Db2, Cassandra, and Vitess out of the box. Run mode: deploy as Kafka Connect workers, or use Debezium Server (standalone) if you don't want a Kafka Connect cluster. WAL = Write-Ahead Log: the database's commit-ordered durable log that already exists for replication and crash recovery; Debezium just subscribes to it.

find: Expand the 'three pillars' framing into the five signals modern observability uses. Traces answer where the time went and which hop failed in one request. Metrics answer the trend question — aggregate rates, errors, latencies over time (the RED method: Rate, Errors, Duration; the USE method: Utilisation, Saturation, Errors). Logs answer what exactly happened in one component. Baggage is the signal most people miss — it's key-value context (tenant_id, user_tier, feature_flag) that propagates along the whole trace, so a value set at the edge is readable in a Kafka consumer three hops downstream. Profiles are the newest signal — continuous CPU / memory / lock sampling per service, answering which function is burning the CPU (Pyroscope, Parca, Grafana Phlare). The correlation bar at the bottom is the whole point: traces, metrics, logs, baggage and profiles all share trace_id + span_id + resource attributes (service.name, k8s.pod.name, deployment.version), so you can pivot — a metric spike leads to an exemplar trace, which leads to its logs, which leads to its CPU profile. OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral SDK and wire format for all five; traces/metrics/logs are GA, baggage is stable, profiling is the newest (the OTel profiling signal reached the ecosystem in 2024).

find: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) is the pattern of using different models for writes and reads. The write side optimises for invariants and consistency: a normalised schema in a transactional store (Postgres, MySQL). The read side optimises for query shape: denormalised wide tables, an Elasticsearch index, a Mongo document, or whatever fits the question being asked. The two are linked by a stream of events: either domain events emitted by the write side, or the database commit log itself via CDC, the log-tailing pattern. The cost: eventual consistency, a small lag between the write committing and the read model catching up. The benefit: each side can scale, schema-evolve and even be stored independently. Use this pattern when reads and writes have different shapes and access patterns. Avoid it when a single store handles both; CQRS adds operational complexity that isn't free. The classic motivating case: a service that takes thousands of writes per second but is read by analytics, dashboards and search — the write model serves the writes, the read model serves the rest. CQRS pairs naturally with event sourcing on the write side and event streaming for projections; the Event-Driven section draws both distinctions.

find: Auto-injection, auto-instrumentation and manual instrumentation are three things people conflate. Manual: you call the tracer API yourself; necessary for domain operations. Auto-instrumentation: the OTel instrumentation libraries (or a language agent) wrap known frameworks: your HTTP handler, your DB driver, your Kafka client all emit spans without you touching them. Auto-injection: a Kubernetes-level mechanism; the OpenTelemetry Operator sees a pod annotation and injects the language agent + config as an init container / env vars at admission time, so you don't even put the agent in your image. Per-language specifics: Python: 'opentelemetry-instrument' wrapper or the operator injects it; instrumentation packages per library. Java/Quarkus: the OTel Java agent (-javaagent) auto-instruments everything; Quarkus also has build-time OTel extension. Spring: Micrometer Tracing + the OTel bridge, or the Java agent. .NET: OTel auto-instrumentation via the OpenTelemetry.AutoInstrumentation package or the operator's .NET injection; manual via System.Diagnostics.ActivitySource. The bold line is the mental model: injection delivers the agent, the agent instruments frameworks, you add manual spans on top — they layer into one trace.

find: Demystify the magic word 'correlation.' It is not a backend join — it's the trace context physically travelling with the request, in-band, at every hop. The W3C traceparent header is the standard: version-traceid-parentspanid-flags. The trace_id (16 bytes) is constant across every hop of the request — that constancy is literally what stitches the distributed story into one trace. The span_id is new per operation, and each span records its parent span_id, which is how the backend rebuilds the tree. The flags byte carries the sampling decision (01 = sampled) so every hop honours the same decision. Alongside traceparent rides tracestate (vendor-specific) and baggage (your key-values). The transport differs per hop but the mechanism is identical: HTTP uses the traceparent header, gRPC uses metadata, Kafka uses message headers. The SDK injects the context on the way out and extracts it on the way in — automatically, which is why auto-instrumentation 'just works' across services. This propagated context is exactly why the same trace_id shows up on the trace waterfall, on every structured log line, and as an exemplar on your metrics — they all read it from the same in-band context.

find: The decision guide for sampling. Probabilistic is the simplest and the most common starting point — keep 10%, predictable volume. Rate-limiting is better when traffic is bursty because it caps absolute volume. Parent-based is non-negotiable in a distributed system: without it, service A samples a trace but service B independently drops it, and you get a broken trace with holes — worse than no trace. Tail-based sampling gives the most control: because the Collector sees the whole trace before deciding, it can guarantee you keep every error and every slow request, which are the traces you want during an incident. The cost is the Collector must buffer in-flight traces (memory) and evaluate rules (CPU), and it must see all spans of a trace (which constrains how you load-balance the Collector — use a trace-ID-aware load balancer). The recommended setup combines head (for a cheap representative baseline) and tail (for guaranteed capture of the interesting traces). The sub-bullet is the reminder: traces, metrics and logs are sampled differently — you never sample a metric counter, and logs typically follow their own retention or are sampled to match their parent trace.

find: Tight, complete. The decorator is a real FastAPI app. The GET path adds a Redis cache with a 60-second TTL — a capability the legacy service didn't have. The POST path delegates the actual write to the legacy service (it's still the source of truth), then emits a Kafka event so downstream systems can subscribe to the new event stream, then invalidates the cache. The legacy service has no idea it's been wrapped; clients have no idea they're talking to a decorator. Over time you can move more behaviour into the decorator: validation rules, idempotency keys, dedup, multi-source reads. When you're ready to retire the legacy service, you implement the order storage inside the decorator (or in a clean new service it calls) and stop forwarding — the API stays the same for clients. This is also the right shape for adding capabilities your vendor can't provide, such as PII redaction, retention policies or multi-region failover, to a system you can't modify. find: Six patterns that all share the same L7 primitives. Canary: 90/10 weighted routing to a new version, watching metrics and ramping. Blue/green: two identical environments, traffic flipped atomically (and rolled back atomically). Shadow / mirror: copy a percentage of real traffic to a new version, observe its behaviour, but don't return its responses to the client; this tests the new version under realistic load. find: Splitting the database is the hard part of decomposition: schema dependencies, cross-table joins, and reporting queries all create coupling that stays invisible until you try to move data. The insight of this pattern: do that work while you're still one process. Each module gets its own Postgres / Mongo / whatever, its own connection pool, its own migration history. Cross-module data is now async or event-driven — you replace a JOIN with a service call or an event subscription. Same discipline microservices require, but with one operational target instead of N. Once this is done, promoting a module to a separate service is a refactor of the deployment topology, not a data-migration project. (Many teams discover at this point that they don't need separate services: the modular monolith with decomposed data is enough.) Practical tip: start with the highest-coupling module first; the second hardest is the database that the reporting layer joins across, so do that one early.

find: See the diagram notes. Amplification is a positive feedback loop: the system's own defensive behaviour (retrying) becomes the attack. Two compounding effects. First, retry multiplication across layers: if the gateway retries 3x, and it calls a service that retries 3x, which calls a service that retries 3x, one user request becomes 27 requests to the bottom of the stack. Second, synchronisation: every client that failed at the same moment retries at the same moment, creating a thundering herd. The result can be metastable — the system stays collapsed even after the original trigger is gone, because the retry load alone sustains the failure. Breaking it: exponential backoff with jitter (de-synchronise), retry budgets (cap retries to a small percentage of live traffic so they can never multiply unboundedly), retry at exactly one layer, and circuit breakers to stop the doomed calls entirely. This is the failure mode most often caused by well-intentioned resilience code.

VirtualService configures per-route timeouts and retries (with Envoy adding backoff and jitter automatically, and retryOn conditions controlling which failures are retried). That is exactly the gray-failure defence the health-check can't provide. The important discipline: don't double up. If Istio is retrying, don't also retry in the app (that's amplification). Decide where each concern lives — typically: timeouts and outlier detection at the mesh, business-aware retries and fallbacks in the app.

Pros: dramatically less data through the application (memory, bandwidth, latency); no long-lived credentials at the client; no app-side credential to leak; the token can expire and be revoked. Cons: requires the storage side to validate tokens; the token's permissions and TTL must be carefully scoped — a leaked token still has its window. Every implementation has the same shape: sign the operation, the object key and the expiry with a key the storage side can check. Example 12 mints and verifies such a ticket in the service itself (HMAC-SHA256, an HS256 JWT in Go and C++), and most object stores, open-source ones included, accept signed URLs of the same shape. The code shows the pattern in the service's language.

find: The fastest-write pattern, with the most caveats. The client writes to the cache and gets an immediate ack — the cache is the source of truth for that window. A background process drains the cache to the DB, batching writes for efficiency. Pros: write latency equals cache latency — microseconds, not milliseconds; massive throughput on write-heavy workloads. Cons: a cache crash before the flusher catches up loses unflushed writes; the cache must be configured for persistence (Redis AOF or RDB snapshots), and even then you might lose seconds of data. Reads from outside the cache (analytics, BI) lag by the flush interval. Use this pattern only when (a) write throughput is the constraint, (b) eventual durability is acceptable, and (c) you've worked out what 'lost the last 5 seconds of writes' means for your business. Common: real-time gaming state, IoT telemetry with a downstream aggregator, write-heavy buffering before a slower backing store.

The old model (top of the diagram) was 'get inside the VPN, everything inside is trusted': once an attacker is in, they move laterally with little resistance. A breach in one service gives you nothing because the next call still has to prove identity and pass policy.

find: See the diagram notes. Cascading failure is how a single slow dependency takes down an entire system. The mechanism: a slow database causes the calling service's request threads (or async tasks, or connection pool) to fill up waiting; with its resources exhausted, that service now fails or slows for all callers, not just the ones touching the database; its callers' resources then fill up waiting on it; and so on up the graph until the user-facing edge is down. The amplifiers are synchronous call chains and unbounded resources (unbounded queues, unbounded thread pools, no timeouts). Each defensive pattern breaks one link: timeouts stop threads blocking forever; bulkheads isolate the pool so the database calls can't consume all of it; circuit breakers stop calling the slow dependency entirely; load shedding rejects excess work at the edge before it propagates. This is the failure mode bulkheads (section 12) were invented for.

find: Bulkhead: borrowed from naval architecture, where watertight compartments stop one breach from sinking the ship. In software, you isolate resources (connection pools, thread pools, async semaphores, queues) by tenant, by call type, or by priority. The left side of the diagram (red) shows the default: one shared pool means a single tenant's traffic storm starves everyone else's. The right side: separate pools, each with its own bounded size. A storm from tenant A consumes tenant A's pool and rejects further A requests — tenants B and background workloads keep running. Why this matters for security as well as resilience: a compromised tenant or a compromised endpoint can be used to mount a denial-of-service against the shared system; bulkheads cap that to its own pool. Implementations: Resilience4j Bulkhead (JVM), Polly (.NET), asyncio.Semaphore (Python), Istio per-destination connection pools at the mesh layer.

find: Three modes worth knowing about. No affinity is the default and what you want — any pod gets any request, load is even, and client state lives somewhere else (Redis, the JWT, the database). Cookie-based stickiness is what you fall back to when something stateful (a shopping cart in memory, a legacy session) has to stay with one pod; the LB sets a cookie on the first response and uses it to route subsequent requests to the same pod. It works behind any L7 LB but ties the user's session to one pod's lifetime — restart that pod, lose the session. IP-hash hashes the source IP to a pod; it needs no cookies but is fragile to NAT and mobile networks where many users share an IP, leading to skewed load. The red footer is the real cost: stickiness fights elastic scaling, hurts pod restarts and breaks scale-to-zero. Use it only for a known constraint, never as a default.

find: This is the failure mode that turns a brief blip into a full outage. The loop: a service slows, calls start timing out, clients retry (often 3x), which triples the load on the already-struggling service, causing more timeouts, causing more retries. It's a positive feedback loop, and naive retry logic is the amplifier. The controls that break it, bottom of the slide: bound every call with a timeout; cap retries to a small number and only for idempotent calls; space them with exponential backoff plus jitter (so clients don't retry in lockstep); add a circuit breaker to fail fast while the dependency is down; enforce a retry budget (cap retries as a percentage of traffic); and shed load early with 429/UNAVAILABLE rather than queueing work you can't do. The Istio config from section 2 provides several of these at the mesh layer without code changes.

find: See the diagram notes. Two ideas. First, every remote call must have a timeout — the default in many HTTP clients is infinite, which is how a single slow dependency hangs a whole service. Second, deadline propagation: the original deadline (say 1000ms) travels with the request, and each hop subtracts the time it has used and passes the remainder downstream. When the remaining budget is too small to plausibly finish, the downstream fails immediately rather than starting work that will be thrown away. gRPC does this natively with deadlines; for HTTP you pass a deadline header and honour it. The waste this prevents is real: without it, your database spends 500ms on a query for a request the user abandoned 450ms ago, and that wasted work is exactly what tips an overloaded system over. The code example shows the language-specific mechanics.

find: When stale reads are not acceptable, write-through forces every write to update both stores atomically (or as close to atomically as you can manage). The application calls cache.set(...) and db.update(...) and both must succeed before the response returns. find: Two flavours of write-through. The first reads back the row from the DB after update and caches that row — the canonical value, including any server-side defaults, triggers, or computed columns. The second writes the request body directly to the cache, which is faster (one less DB round trip) but the cached value may diverge from the DB if the DB applies server-side modifications you didn't replicate. Pick by your DB schema's complexity. Either way, the DB write goes first because the DB is the source of truth — if the cache write fails, you've lost cache freshness but not data. If the DB write fails, you return an error and don't touch the cache. The TTL is your safety net: even if cache and DB diverge briefly, they'll re-converge when the cache entry expires and the next read re-populates from the DB.

find: Two related patterns that often get skipped. Load shedding is counter-intuitive to engineers, because rejecting requests feels like giving up, but it is the difference between a system that degrades and one that collapses. The maths is simple: if you are at 120% of capacity and accept everything, everything is slow and timing out (0% goodput); if you shed the excess 20%, the 80% you accept is served well. Adaptive limiters do this automatically based on latency. Graceful degradation is the product-level decision about what to return when you can't return everything — it requires the product/design team's input on what's essential vs nice-to-have. The bold line ties shedding, breakers and fallback together as a system: stop accepting (shed), stop calling (break), return something useful (fall back).

find: gRPC has a few sharp edges of its own. Route on the gRPC URI prefix to do per-method canaries. Use least-request (or random-3-choices) load balancing instead of round-robin because gRPC connections are long-lived — a few long-running streams can starve other backends if you round-robin connections instead of requests. Be careful with retries on streaming RPCs: the mesh can retry a UNARY call safely if it's idempotent, but retrying a half-completed streaming RPC will replay half the work — Istio lets you scope retries to specific gRPC status codes and request kinds. find: See the diagram notes. Split-brain is the specific catastrophic outcome of a partition in a system that elects a leader or primary. Both sides lose contact, each assumes the other died, each promotes itself, and now you have two primaries accepting conflicting writes. On heal you have divergent state and no clean way to merge. The prevention is quorum: an action requires a majority (N/2 + 1) of nodes to agree, so a minority partition mathematically cannot act — it knows it is the minority and steps down. This is why cluster sizes are odd (3, 5, 7): to always have a clear majority. Fencing tokens (monotonically increasing IDs that let resources reject a stale leader's writes) and leases are complementary. etcd/Raft give the Kubernetes control plane this property out of the box.

find: Set the frame. The single most important conceptual shift for developers moving from monoliths is partial failure: in a monolith a function call either returns or throws, synchronously, in-process. Across a network there is a whole spectrum of failure, including the worst kind — the call that hangs, or the one that succeeded on the server but whose response was lost, leaving the client unsure whether to retry. Emphasise that failures are correlated (one failure causes others) and that some failures are actively deceptive (gray failures). Land the bold point hard: we are not trying to prevent failure, we are trying to bound it and recover. This reframes everything that follows from 'how do we stop failures' to 'how do we contain and survive them.'

find: The audience point: the sidecar pattern works only if the app uses the headers the sidecar attaches. The most common failure mode is an app that ignores X-Forwarded-Client-Cert and falls back to 'allow if you got here.' Make the headers required, not optional. The second-most-common failure mode is forgetting that traffic can sometimes bypass the sidecar (port-forward for debugging, host networking, direct pod-to-pod calls within the same node). With both the sidecar and the NetworkPolicy, the app can fully trust the headers and become much simpler — no crypto code, no JWT parsing library, just header reads.

find: Integration strength has four levels, worst to best. Intrusive coupling: one component reaches into another's private internals — the classic case is two services on one database, where either can break the other invisibly. Functional coupling: they share business logic or rules and must change together for functional reasons. Model coupling: they share a data model or DTOs — a shared library of types. Contract coupling: they integrate only through an explicit, stable, versioned contract — and that's our REST, gRPC, GraphQL and Kafka schemas in the registry. Lower on the ladder means less shared knowledge and looser coupling. The rule that matters: the greater the distance between two components, the further down this ladder you need to be.

find: HAProxy is the lingua franca of L7 LBs. The pattern is always the same: declare ACLs that read parts of the L7 envelope (path_beg for URL prefixes, hdr/req.hdr for headers, content-type for the body type), then use_backend dispatches based on those ACLs in order. find: When data is written far more often than it's read (audit logs, event records, telemetry), caching every write is wasteful: most cached entries expire before being read again. Write-around solves this: write the DB, leave the cache alone. The next reader pays the cache-miss cost and populates the cache. Pros: no cache pollution by write-only data; the cache holds only what is being read. Cons: the first read after every write is slow (cache miss); reads of recently-written data are slower than under cache-aside. Pair with cache-aside or read-through on the read side. Common use: any 'append-only' or 'mostly-written' workload — events, log lines, audit entries, IoT telemetry where you read summaries, not individual entries.

find: The cloud-native posture: treat every connection as disposable and design for its loss. Heartbeats (ping/pong) detect a dead link quickly — TCP alone can hang for minutes. When the connection drops, the client reconnects with exponential backoff plus jitter (so ten thousand clients don't reconnect in lockstep and hammer your pods after a rollout). On reconnect, the client sends its last-seen sequence number (last_seq = 1042); the server replays only the events the client missed (1043 onward), and because each frame carries a seq, the client can dedupe — so the whole thing is at-least-once and idempotent. The principle on screen: resume, don't restart. A reconnect should be invisible to the user, not a full state reload.

find: GraphQL breaks the one-request-one-status assumption: a single query can touch many resolvers, so the response is almost always HTTP 200 and carries both a data object and an errors array. When one field fails (say stock can't reach inventory), that field is set to null, an entry is added to errors[] with a message and the path to the failed field, and the machine code goes in extensions.code along with retryable and traceId. The rest of the data still returns. The anti-pattern to call out: blanket-failing the whole query (or returning a 500) when only one field broke — that throws away useful data the client already asked for. Partial success is a feature; let the client decide whether to retry just the failed field.

find: The pattern that makes WebSockets horizontally scalable. Each pod still owns only its own sockets, which is fine, but every pod subscribes and publishes to a shared backplane: Redis pub/sub for low latency, or a Kafka topic if you want durability and replay. When a publisher wants to push order.updated to user X, it publishes to the backplane without knowing which pod holds X; the backplane fans the message to all pods, and the one pod that holds X's socket delivers it. Now scale-up and zero-downtime rollouts work again, because no pod is the single home of a conversation — connections can land anywhere and still receive everything. Redis is the common default; Kafka if you already run it and want the durability.

find: Kafka error handling has a failure mode unique to logs: a single poison record can block the whole partition forever if you keep retrying it in place, because the offset never advances — head-of-line blocking that stalls every record behind it. You commit the offset either way, so the main consumer keeps making progress. The DLQ record carries the original payload plus error and trace headers.

The database commit is the single source of truth. The outbox write itself is one database transaction, shown in code.
